title: Humanity's Impossible Quest for the Truth: Nietzsche's Philosophical Crusade Aga...
summary: Relaunching The Educated Barbarian in a new chapter-summary format, NH covers chapter 1 of Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil: the will to truth, the false hierarchy between truth and untruth, subjectivity, the will to power, utilitarian philosophy, psychology's role and sensualist versus Platonist thinking. It is pure philosophy with no training content.
claims: The Educated Barbarian moves from line-by-line readings to denser chapter summaries; Beyond Good and Evil gets nine episodes released every two weeks on Tuesdays, followed by Jung
Philosophers have always been driven by a will to truth that is both their source and their goal, a paradox that leaves truth undefined
Either truth doesn't exist or humans can't find it; we chase it like a dog chasing a car that wouldn't know what to do if it caught it
Untruth is easier to access than truth, yet we demonize it; perhaps truth and untruth share a source and rejecting one blocks the other
Philosophers assume that things of the highest value must originate from themselves, like God, which makes it impossible to locate where truth comes from
Assigning value to truth and lies on emotional grounds is a mistake; negative emotions like hatred have easily traced origins while romanticized love is never examined
Truth is valued pragmatically because it aids survival, like knowing which water is safe to drink, and permanence brings stability
Instinct is the purest form of reason; correct ideas are usually felt instinctively first and argued for afterwards
A false opinion is only a problem if it isn't life-furthering; renouncing all false opinions would mean renouncing life
Don't place good above evil in a hierarchy: put them on equal footing and ask what makes something virtuous
Every human statement is subjective; those who claim pure objectivity deceive you and themselves, and refusing to accept bias is rhetorical weakness
The will to truth is an instrument of the will to power: being right gives you the upper hand
Though he aligns with Stoicism, he accepts Nietzsche's critique that Stoics projected their ideal onto nature and then claimed to live according to it
Preferring a handful of certainties to uncertain possibilities leads to nihilism, belief in a sure nothing; he argues atheism is not a belief system
Skepticism's acceptance of nuance shows a livelier soul, but distrusting your own senses and the body goes too far
Religious people rightly perceive truths beyond human reach, but trying to return to the past fails; philosophy must push forward
The soul should neither be accepted as unquestionable truth nor dismissed as myth, but examined for its value
Psychology became a timid soft science; it should treat the will to power, not self-preservation, as the core instinct
Psychology explains why moral rules exist (e.g. the incest taboo protects bloodlines) and philosophy explains how to live them; Nietzsche questioned morality rather than hating it
Sensualism (trust only the senses) is plebeian and Platonism (conceptual networks) aristocratic, but the senses are the rocket launcher thought can never fully discard
Descartes' 'I think therefore I am' is circular and leads nowhere
